The paper proposes OpenAGI, a framework for testing and training existing and future AGI models (here, for example, those that can take in or output either text or images).
OpenAGI is based on the idea that large language models (LLMs) now can read task instructions in a sentence (e.g. "restore this image", and generate a list of steps for solving the task (akin to AutoGPT). The framework is a closed loop that starts from (1) reading task instructions; (2) generating a list of steps toward the solution; (3) utilizing existing tools to execute each step; and (4) generating results.
In such a closed loop, LLMs can be fine-tuned using a set of objective measures defined by the generated results, i.e. no humans in the loop or Reinforcement Learning from Task Feedback (RLTF).

This paper is more like ViperGPT and AutoGPT, yet, applied to testing and training AI models themselves.
The work is quite thorough: exploring 6 different input/output settings; 6 different LLMs. The framework also shows that significant performance improvements can be observed for Vicuna-7b and Flan-T5-Large when fine-tuning or using RLTF compared to zero-shot and few-shot learning methods.

The work is solid and thorough. The framework and its code can practically contribute to the community.
Dear reviewer, we very much appreciate your clarification. Thank you.

We appreciate your suggestion of adding more related works and we agree LLM agents for complex task-solving has been an important topic recently. Actually, this also demonstrates the importance of our project as an attempt to benchmark the complex task-solving ability of LLMs. However, most of the LLM agent works appeared very recently just in the past one or two months and mostly after the NeurIPS submission was due. During the development period of our project from Fall 2022 up to the NeurIPS submission deadline, we were unaware of most of the current LLM agent works except for those ones that we have already cited in the paper. However, as mentioned, we appreciate your suggestion and we will add more related works on LLM agent studies, which should be a easy fix to the paper.

We also appreciate your question on 'OpenAGI' and we hope to provide more discussions and clarifications on this. We honestly believe OpenAGI is a legitimate name for the project, and this is because of following three reasons.

1) Our project not only supports benchmark tasks but also supports open-ended tasks. The benchmark tasks are important because we hope to contribute to the community with a standard way of evaluating the complex task-solving ability of LLMs. Based on the experimental results shown in the paper and in the discussion period, even 'scheduling an image processing workflow' is not an easy task for most state-of-the-art LLMs such as GPT-4 and LLaMA. Furthermore, the open-ended task mode allows users to create basically any task using natural language for the platform to solve. Once the platform solves the user created tasks and presents the solution to users, users are allowed to provide feedback on the task-solving quality. Once these tasks are created and user feedback is collected, they will be saved into the task database under user consent, which allows the platform to collect and share more and more real-world tasks with their ground-truth labels. As a result, by design, the platform has no restriction on the type of problems to solve, and we envision this as a dynamic process to establish a virtuous circle between humans and AI.

2) Our project takes a very inclusive design from the beginning, which allows future AI advancement to be easily integrated into the framework. More specifically, we understand that there may be different AI development philosophies in the community, such as connectionism, symbolism, empiricism and rationalism, however, no matter for neural models, symbolic models, planning models, reasoning models or any other models, they can be easily integrated into the framework as expert models, and future improvements on LLM such as its reasoning and planning ability can also be integrated by upgrading the LLM backbone. Furthermore, the framework also supports human interaction and intervention in the process. As a result, our project does not exclude any possible approach towards AGI.

3) We are not the only one to follow an AGI type of naming for relevant projects. Except for our project, there are other recent projects such as BabyAGI, SuperAGI, MiniAGI, BigAGI, etc. which also follow an AGI type of naming. Our project has differences from these ones in that we support both benchmarking tasks and open-ended tasks, as well as an innovative Reinforcement Learning from Task Feedback (RLTF) mechanism to enable LLMs' self-improvement from task-solving experiences. However, as mentioned above, we appreciate your suggestion and we will cite and discuss these projects in the related work of the paper. Finally, we would like to thank you for acknowledging our evaluations on GPT-4, Claude-2, and Llama-2.

Thank you for your valuable feedback and suggestions. We have included additional related work on RLHF in our 'Related Work' section, since it is closely related to our proposed method, RLTF. We’ve also added AutoGPT, BabyAGI and many other related Github repos into this section.

We acknowledge the importance of broadening the diversity and range of expert models to enhance the adaptability and scalability of our platform. However, we have limited the size of such a model set for a few reasons. Firstly, maintaining a manageable set size allows for feasible benchmarking, given that the selection of expert models is largely dictated by the available datasets. For instance, while we could incorporate a search engine into the model set, there is not a suitable public dataset for benchmarking such an expert model. Secondly, the Large Language Models (LLMs) like Flan-T5 and Llama have constraints on context length, which are limited to 512 tokens and 2k tokens, respectively. Adding more models could easily exceed these constraints, especially when model names or descriptions are included in the prompt.

Considering the new architecture issue, on one hand, this work primarily emphasizes the data and benchmark perspective. Consequently, the goal is not to design new LLM architectures. Instead, we evaluated various existing and widely used LLMs under different learning schemas. Our findings suggest that there is substantial potential for research in this area, given that many existing methods underperform. On the other hand, except for zero-shot learning, few-shot learning, and fine-tuning, we have implemented an innovative RLTF mechanism for modeling training to show the performance of various LLMs under different learning schemas. Furthermore, we have benchmarked even more LLMs for greater comprehensiveness, please kindly refer to the next part of this response for detailed results.

Given the limitations highlighted in our study, we believe it is essential for the community to establish a benchmark for LLMs on complex task solving, which is the very purpose of this research. Subsequent research on these limitations can then be built upon the dataset, benchmark, and framework. Moreover, we have also provided the constrained generation framework in the project to help mitigate such negative effects, which allows users to freely configure the constraints in the plan generation process of LLMs so as to regulate the generated plans.

We also appreciate your skepticism about the value of benchmarking LLMs and domain expert models on complex task solving as a route towards AGI, and we believe that healthy debates on this topic is important. We acknowledge that as an initial effort, there is certainly room to improve our project’s quality and adoption as a widely used benchmark. However, OpenAGI is not a tool or software project, instead, we focus on evaluating the reasoning and planning ability of LLMs. Moreover, we respectfully disagree that this offers limited contribution or impact. This benchmarking serves several important purposes:\
•	It enables standardized measurement of capabilities and progress across the research community. Lack of unified benchmarks hampers advancement.\
•	Analyzing model performance on composed tasks provides insights into emergent abilities from combining skills - an essential aspect of general intelligence.\
•	Benchmarking on expansive tasks helps identify current method limitations to guide research directions.\
•	Availability of an open benchmark facilitates faster reproduction and apples-to-apples comparison of techniques by different groups.\
•	Quantifying capabilities on complex human-relevant tasks, even if imperfect, keeps research grounded in real-world utility.

We sincerely appreciate it that you highlighting this point - it helps us to improve the clarity and thoroughness of our methodology description.

The performance metrics for RLTF are derived from the test set, we sample 10% of the remaining task (14 tasks) for testing. We repeat the sampling and testing process for several rounds to calculate the average performance. These tasks were randomly chosen, distinct from the training tasks.
The improved performance could be attributed to:
1) Initializing RLTF with weights from the fine-tuned model, which were already of high quality;
2) RL introduces the ability of exploration when generating models, which is a crucial factor;
3) The training tasks encompass all expert models in our dataset, thereby better assisting the learning of LLM.

summary_and_contributions.value: This work introduces OpenAGI, an open-source AGI research platform designed for multi-step, real-world tasks. The authors have argued that the existing works have three major problems: (1) only work for a fixed number of models (2) limited to solving tasks with linear task-planning solutions, meaning that each sub-task must be completed before the next sub-task can start, no modalities, etc. (3) only provide qualitative results. The benchmark tasks (as described in Figure 1) are those that have specific objectives and their performance can be gauged by a specific benchmark, such as image-to-text or text-to-image. The open-ended tasks (as described in Figure 2), as the name suggested, are those more oriented towards subjective evaluations, such as music and poem generation. This paper also discuss the model fine-tuning method of Reinforcement Learning from Task Feedback (RLTF), and some experiment results have been provided.

strengths.value: - The topic of LLM-based agents is important and worth-exploring

opportunities_for_improvement.value:
- **The paper's clarity could be improved significantly**. Please refer to the 'additional feedback' section for a list of queries regarding your experiments. The scope of the experiments and evaluations conducted in this study seems somewhat limited in my view.
- The project does not give the impression of being long-term. Questions arise regarding the software quality, maintainability, and consequently, the long-term reliability of this platform. There seems to be a lack of rigorous QA/QC, evidenced by the absence of GitHub actions, build, and test routines. No active updates have been noted in the GitHub Repo since mid-June, hinting at a somewhat static user community
- In 'Plan Execution' as presented in Figures 1 and 2, the authors offer screenshots from GitHub Repos (not their own) in an attempt to demonstrate the pipeline's functionality. This method lacks convincing power. A more compelling approach could be to replace screenshots with informative data visualizations.

limitations.value: The discussion of limitations should be moved to the main text.

correctness.value: The pipeline seems constructed in a sound way.

clarity.value: The paper's readability could be enhanced significantly, as it currently lacks certain essential details, making it difficult to follow. Improvements in the presentation and organization of the content are necessary to bolster the paper's quality. The details regarding the RLTF algorithm and the experiment setup are not included in the main text, and they shouldn't be put in the appendix.

relation_to_prior_work.value: There are many existing works on LLM-based agents (i.e. where LLM is used in planning and completing downstream tasks), I think the authors should at least discuss the existences of publicly-available GitHub repos such as Auto-GPT and "ChatGPT for Robotics" by Microsoft at the related work section. I don't see how this work is too different from those LLM-based agents. I think you could similarly call the different configurations (e.g. image generation, web search) in Auto-GPT a set of "domain expert skills".

documentation.value: Looks like there are a sufficient amount of details provided on the GitHub repo to reproduce the results. I have yet to confirm if the code can work without any issues.

**Questions regarding the experiments:**
- I am fairly confused when I am reading through the experiment section. It remains unclear what tasks the authors sought to benchmark. Given the presence of numerous vision-language alignment metrics, such as CLIP, BERT, and ViT scores, one might infer that the tasks were related to text-to-image alignment. If that is the case, further details (e.g. size of the evaluation dataset) on the experiment's execution are needed to fully understand the methodology employed.
- As I have mentioned above, CLIP, BERT, and ViT scores are metrics mainly used in image-captioning - to test text-to-image alignments. They are not perfect nor comprehensive enough for evaluating the generalization of your method in any way. Consider incorporating a wider array of metrics and conducting evaluations on a broader range of downstream tasks. This will enhance the comprehensiveness and robustness of your evaluation, thereby strengthening the paper's validity and reliability.

summary_and_contributions.value:
This paper introduces the OpenAGI platform for benchmarking LLMs for open-domain model synthesis (OMS): creating plans to utilise multiple expert models to solve complex tasks. The platform has a variety of tasks enabled by a variety of expert models (other AI models, as well as other functionality), where each task consists of a task description and a set of inputs. The LLM takes the task description as input, and produces a plan using the expert models which can be applied to each input in term to produce an output. The platform consists of benchmark tasks with ground-truth outputs which can be used to automatically (using neural evaluation metrics), and open-ended tasks which require human evaluation.

The authors also introduce RLTF, which involves fine-tuning a model with the automated task feedback provided by the ground truth outputs using reinforcement learning.

The paper benchmarks chatGPT, Vicuna-7B and T5-Flan in a zero-shot, few-shot, supervised fine-tuning and RLTF setup. They show that ChatGPT performs well zero-shot and few-shot, while other models generally require some form of additional fine-tuning to perform well. The T5-flan model after supervised fine-tuning and RLTF outperforms chatgpt few-shot despite being much smaller.

strengths.value: Open-domain model synthesis is an exciting research area that definitely lacks benchmarks, and so this benchmark platform is very relevant and necessary. The paper is easy to read and mostly clear, especially in the graphical representation of the platform. There are quite a large range of tasks, and the method of creating tasks from data augmentation techniques and combining existing expert models is interesting and could be useful in other settings as well.

opportunities_for_improvement.value:
I think the paper's weaknesses are in 4 main areas:

# Unnatural task set

While the idea of creating a set of OMS tasks from existing expert models is interesting, these tasks don't seem like natural tasks that users are likely to ask general-purpose AI models. Particularly tasks like "Given two reviews of a movie in English, translate them into German and provide a summary" seem unlikely to be something users would require models to do. The fact that the set of tasks isn't sourced from a study of what users would actually want from OMS models limits the benchmarks usefulness in making sure methods for OMS are actually improving the things we want them to be improving.

This could be improved by creating a more natural task set, particularly where it's immediately obvious which expert models should be used for the task, to test for more open-ended problem solving and planning in LLMs.

# Limited benchmarking of existing models

While 3 models are benchmarked, it would be beneficial to benchmark additional models, both closed-source (claude, gpt4) and open-source (base llama models, larger llama variants, etc.). Additionally, an expert human baseline would be useful to understand how well qualitatively speaking these models are actually doing - the reported scores don't lend themselves to easy interpretation.

# No analysis of successes and failures of methods and models

While it's interesting that T5-Flan with supervised fine-tuning and RLTF outperforms few-shot ChatGPT, there is no analysis of why this is the case, what the plans look like for these models, in what ways they are succeeding or failing, and what open problems remain that these models can't currently do well on. This would enable more targeted future work on this benchmark and help us understand why different methods succeed or fail.

Human evaluations would additionally be useful here to understand how well each model is performing.

# Lack of detail for the benchmark

There is a lack of clarity about how some parts of the benchmark are implemented, for example whether the prompt only includes relevant expert models or all of them, and exactly how the outputted plan of the model is parsed and passed to the expert models. This could be served by better documentation in the github repository.

# Summary

Overall, I think the paper isn't currently worthy of acceptance, but that it could be improved in the rebuttal period by addressing some of the points above. I'd raise my score to 6 if more models were benchmarked and more analysis of the model's performance was done, and I'd raise it further if a more natural distribution of tasks was used and human evaluations were performed.

UPDATE: based on the benchmarking of additional models and analysis in the author's response, I have raised my score to a 6.

limitations.value: The authors spend a short paragraph addressing the limitations in the supplementary material, but I think they can spend more effort discussing the limitations of the benchmark in terms of the kinds of tasks it considers, the lack of human evaluations for open-ended tasks, the lack of investigation into how RLTF performs well and what the outputs of T5-flan work, and whether the training method would perform well under distribution shift.

correctness.value: All the claims in the paper are correct. There's no analysis or representation of the training and testing sets, so it's unclear how similar they are and to what extend models are memorising patterns specific to the platform rather than learning general-purpose behaviour.

documentation.value: The code, data and models are released, which is good, but the documentation for the code is very limited, and doesn't show how to benchmark a new model or adjust the training. The code doesn't include a maintenance plan

additional_feedback.value:
* Citations are incorred in the first paragraph of page 4 (toolformer is cited with hugginggpt and vice versa)
* It's not known how many parameters GPT 3.5 has, so you can't say it's >175 billion.
* "Possible explanation for this may be Vicuna-7b’s greater data requirements due to its larger model size (as we only used 18 human-labelled data samples for training)." Generally work has shown that larger models need less data, so this is unlikely to be the correct explanation.
* In figure 3 you have users who performan human evaluation, but you don't do any human evaluations in the paper, so this is misleading.
* It's unclear from the paper whether the model is provided with the list of all domain expert models in the prompt regardless of which task it's being asked to complete, or whether it only gets the list of domain expert models that are relevant to the task in the prompt. I think testing with the former settings is more realistic, so if this isn't what's done then the paper is less useful, as it implicitly assumes we know which domain-expert models are relevant for a given task. Which is used?
* More qualitative analysis of model outputs in both successful and failing cases would be useful.
* Including a full list of the tasks and corresponding datasets in the supplementary material would be useful, including which tasks are used for training and which for testing.

title.value: OpenAGI: When LLM Meets Domain Experts

abstract.value: Human Intelligence (HI) excels at combining basic skills to solve complex tasks. This capability is vital for Artificial Intelligence (AI) and should be embedded in comprehensive AI Agents, enabling them to harness expert models for complex task-solving towards Artificial General Intelligence (AGI). Large Language Models (LLMs) show promising learning and reasoning abilities, and can effectively use external models, tools, plugins, or APIs to tackle complex problems. In this work, we introduce OpenAGI, an open-source AGI research and development platform designed for solving multi-step, real-world tasks. Specifically, OpenAGI uses a dual strategy, integrating standard benchmark tasks for benchmarking and evaluation, and open-ended tasks including more expandable models, tools, plugins, or APIs for creative problem-solving. Tasks are presented as natural language queries to the LLM, which then selects and executes appropriate models. We also propose a Reinforcement Learning from Task Feedback (RLTF) mechanism that uses task results to improve the LLM's task-solving ability, which creates a self-improving AI feedback loop. While we acknowledge that AGI is a broad and multifaceted research challenge with no singularly defined solution path, the integration of LLMs with domain-specific expert models, inspired by mirroring the blend of general and specialized intelligence in humans, offers a promising approach towards AGI. We are open-sourcing the OpenAGI project's code, dataset, benchmarks, evaluation methods, and the UI demo to foster community involvement in AGI advancement: https://github.com/agiresearch/OpenAGI.

def process(client, invitation):

    domain = client.get_group(invitation.domain)
    venue_id = domain.id
    submission_venue_id = domain.content['submission_venue_id']['value']
    venue_name = domain.content['title']['value']

    now = openreview.tools.datetime_millis(datetime.datetime.utcnow())
    cdate = invitation.cdate

    if cdate > now:
        ## invitation is in the future, do not process
        print('invitation is not yet active', cdate)
        return

    def post_submission_edit(submission):

        updated_note = openreview.api.Note(
            id=submission.id
        )

        if invitation.edit['note']['readers'] == ['everyone'] and submission.odate is None:
            updated_note.odate = now
            updated_note.content = {
                '_bibtex': {
                    'value': openreview.tools.generate_bibtex(
                        note=submission,
                        venue_fullname=venue_name,
                        year=str(datetime.datetime.utcnow().year),
                        url_forum=submission.forum,
                        paper_status='under review',
                        anonymous='readers' in submission.content['authors'] or 'readers' in invitation.edit.get('note', {}).get('content', {}).get('authors', {})
                    )
                }
            }

        client.post_note_edit(
            invitation=invitation.id,
            note=updated_note,
            signatures=[venue_id]
        )
    
    ## Release the submissions to specified readers if venueid is still submission
    submissions = client.get_all_notes(content= { 'venueid': submission_venue_id })
    print(f'update {len(submissions)} submissions')
    openreview.tools.concurrent_requests(post_submission_edit, submissions, desc='post_submission_edit')
